cards.title: Propositional logic: syntax and semantics
cards.hook: Facts + rules in a knowledge base let an agent derive what to do (rain → wet → indoor route).
formula: false only when P = T and Q = F
example: 'If 2 + 2 = 5, then x > 3' is TRUE (vacuously: the premise is false).
cards.memory: Implication is a promise: only broken when the condition happens and the result doesn't.
cards.trap: P ⇒ Q asserts no causation, and is NOT equivalent to Q ⇒ P.
explain: Propositional logic uses symbols (P, Q, …) that are simply true or false, joined by connectives: not ¬, and ∧, or ∨, implies ⇒, if-and-only-if ⇔.
A model assigns true/false to every symbol; the truth table tells you whether a sentence is true in that model.
P ⇒ Q is a promise 'if P then Q'. It is only broken when P is true and Q is false. If P is false the promise can't be broken, so it counts as true ('vacuously true').

tex.t: P \Rightarrow Q \;\equiv\; \neg P \vee Q, \qquad P \Leftrightarrow Q \;\equiv\; (P\Rightarrow Q)\wedge(Q \Rightarrow P)
\neg P \vee Q \wedge R \Rightarrow S \;=\; \big((\neg P) \vee (Q \wedge R)\big) \Rightarrow S

cards.memory: De Morgan: flip the operator, negate each part.
cards.trap: The converse (Q ⇒ P) and inverse (¬P ⇒ ¬Q) are NOT equivalent to P ⇒ Q; only the contrapositive is.
explain: Two sentences are equivalent if they are true in exactly the same models. These rewrite rules let you transform sentences, for example into CNF for resolution, without changing their meaning.

cards.title: First-order logic
cards.hook: FOL talks about objects and ALL/SOME of them in one sentence.
cards.visual:

Quantifier∀x King(x) ⇒ Person(x); ∃x Student(x)–
formula: ∀: any ground term; ∃: one NEW constant
example: EI: ∃x Student(x) ∧ Enrolled(x) → Student(k) ∧ Enrolled(k) with fresh k.
cards.memory: A term names a thing; a sentence is true or false.
cards.trap: Quantifier order matters; EI must use a NEW constant.
explain: First-order logic talks about objects (John, Sydney), properties and relations between them (Student(John), Brother(Richard, John)) and functions that name objects (Father(John)).
Quantifiers let one sentence cover many objects: ∀x (for all x) and ∃x (there exists an x). Pattern: ∀ usually goes with ⇒, ∃ usually goes with ∧.
To reason, propositionalise: replace ∃x by a brand-new constant (EI) and ∀x by specific objects (UI), then use propositional methods.

cards.title: Inference: model checking, theorem proving, resolution
cards.hook: Three ways to show KB ⊨ γ: check every model, chain sound rules, or refute the negation.
formula: list symbols → all models → keep KB-true → check γ
Modus Ponens: P, P ⇒ Q ⊢ Q
example: Rain: only model 1 satisfies KB, and Q is true there → KB ⊨ Q.
Resolution: C1: P, C2: ¬P ∨ Q, C3: ¬Q → resolve C1, C2 → Q; with C3 → □.
cards.memory: Assume the opposite, find the empty box.
cards.trap: Negate ONLY the query (KB ∧ ¬γ), not the KB.
explain: Entailment KB ⊨ γ: whenever everything in the knowledge base is true, γ must be true too.
Model checking: list every truth assignment, keep the ones where the KB is true, and check that γ is true in all of them.

Theorem proving: chain sound rules such as Modus Ponens (P and P ⇒ Q give Q). Resolution: assume the opposite (KB ∧ ¬γ), turn it into clauses, and cancel complementary literals until you reach the empty clause □, a contradiction, which proves KB ⊨ γ.

where: set of models in which α is true
